opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The distinction I find most useful is between two broad categories of risk. The first is where the system is being used as intended but fails in some way: it makes a mistake, hallucinates something that isn't grounded in the source material, or produces content that's harmful or biased even though nobody was trying to make that happen. Those are quality and reliability failures, and we address them by measuring them, improving the model and the system around it, and designing the user experience so people can catch errors.

The second category is adversarial. Someone is deliberately trying to misuse the system or break it. That includes jailbreaks, prompt injection attacks where malicious instructions are hidden in a document or a web page the model reads, and people trying to get the system to produce content it shouldn't. Defending against that looks a lot more like security work: you think about attackers, you red team, you build layered defenses, and you assume people will keep finding new techniques.

Keeping the two separate matters because the mitigations, the measurement approaches, and even the mindset you need are quite different. A lot of real risks sit somewhere in between, of course, but starting with "is this an accidental failure or an intentional attack?" helps us figure out which tools to reach for and makes sure we aren't neglecting either side.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes accidental quality or reliability failures from deliberate adversarial attacks. It does not distinguish risks from undesirable generated content from risks due to problematic model capabilities or limitations; it groups mistakes, hallucinations, harmful content, and bias together.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The distinction that's been most useful for us is separating out whether the AI system is doing something wrong or whether a person is using the system to do something wrong. Those sound similar, but they lead to very different mitigations.

The first bucket is what I'd call the system failing. The model hallucinates, it produces something inaccurate or ungrounded, it generates content that's harmful or biased even though nobody asked it to, it leaks something from its training data or from the context it was given. In those cases the user is often well-intentioned and the technology just didn't do what it should have. The work there is about grounding, about measurement, about building classifiers and filters, about making the system more reliable and more honest about its own uncertainty.

The second bucket is misuse. Here the system may be working exactly as designed, but somebody is deliberately trying to get it to produce something it shouldn't, or using it as a tool to cause harm. That's the jailbreak and prompt injection space, people trying to generate disinformation at scale, attempts to extract capabilities we've intentionally restricted. The mitigations look much more like security work. You think about adversaries, you red team, you build defenses in layers, you monitor for abuse patterns, and you accept that this is an ongoing cat-and-mouse game rather than a problem you solve once.

What I like about this framing is that it keeps us honest. It's tempting to lump everything under "safety" and reach for the same tool every time. But a content filter that stops a model from volunteering harmful material does very little against a determined attacker, and a jailbreak defense doesn't help at all when the model simply made something up for a perfectly innocent user. We also layer a third consideration on top, which is the application context. The same model in a children's education product and in an internal developer tool carries different risk in both buckets. So we ask, for this specific use, what are the ways the system could fail, what are the ways it could be misused, and what does the deployment context tell us about how much each of those matters.

r001.rationale: The response separates system failures—such as hallucinated, harmful, biased, or leaked content—from misuse, where someone exploits the system’s capabilities to cause harm.

astra-6.text: One distinction I find useful is between people intentionally misusing the technology and things going wrong when people are using it as intended. In the first case, someone might be trying to generate harmful content or use the system to support a scam. In the second, someone asks a perfectly reasonable question, but the model gives an inaccurate, biased, or otherwise harmful response. Those require different mitigations: we need to make deliberate abuse harder, while also making the system safer and more reliable for people who are trying to use it appropriately.

r001.rationale: It separates harmful content generated through deliberate misuse from inaccurate, biased, or harmful responses produced during intended use, capturing risks from generated content and model limitations.

sol-6.1.text: One distinction I find useful is between risks that come from the model itself and risks that come from how it’s used. A model might generate harmful or biased content, or produce an answer that sounds convincing but is wrong. Then there are risks from someone deliberately misusing it, or from putting it into an application where a mistake can have serious consequences. That distinction helps us think about what we can address in the model and what needs safeguards in the surrounding system.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes risks from the model itself from risks of its use. It gives generated harmful or biased content and convincing but incorrect answers as model risks, but does not distinguish undesirable generated content from problematic model capabilities or limitations as separate risk categories.
